prompt: What does a JSON Schema check that a JSON parser does not?

choices.text: Field names, types, allowed values and required fields
choices.why: Right. The parser only says the text is JSON; the schema says it is the object you accept.

choices.text: Whether the text is JSON at all
choices.why: That is the parser's job, lesson 18. The validator needs parsed JSON to start from.

choices.text: Whether the values are true
choices.why: No schema reads the complaint. Truth needs the input, as the last reading section shows.

choices.text: Whether the model was confident
choices.why: Nothing in a reply measures confidence, and a schema would not read it if it did.

prompt: `triage/bad-2.json` added a field called `mood`. Which line of the schema made the validator report it?
hint: Which keyword refuses a name the schema did not list?

choices.text: `"required": ["category", "refund", "summary"]`
choices.why: `required` lists fields that must be present. It says nothing about extra ones, and it caught the missing `summary` instead.

choices.text: `"type": "object"`
choices.why: The reply is an object, so that line is satisfied.

choices.text: `"category": {"enum": [...]}`
choices.why: The enum constrains `category`'s value only.

choices.text: `"additionalProperties": false`
choices.why: Yes. Without it, `mood` would pass and travel along unnoticed.

prompt: Why does the validator list all three problems in `bad-1.json` when lesson 18's parser stopped at the first?
hint: What does each tool need before it can look at a field?

choices.text: The validator is a newer, more capable program than Python's parser
choices.why: Age has nothing to do with it. The two answer different questions.

choices.text: It was asked to with a flag
choices.why: `validate` was given no flag. Reporting everything is how it works.

choices.text: The object is already parsed, so every field gets checked
choices.why: Right. Parsing stops where the syntax breaks; validation walks a complete object and reports every rule it breaks.

choices.text: The three problems were on the same line
choices.why: They are in three fields. Lines do not matter once the text is parsed.

prompt: How many problems did `validate` report for `triage/bad-1.json`?
hint: The line before the exit status.

prompt: In a JSON Schema, the keyword ___ lists the only values a field may take, such as the five categories.
The café adds a sixth complaint queue, `hygiene`. The schema is in the prompt and in the program. What is the advantage of that arrangement?
hint: Where would the change have to be made otherwise?

choices.text: One edit updates both, so they cannot disagree
choices.why: Yes. If the prompt described the categories in prose and the program kept its own list, one of the two would be left behind.

choices.text: The model learns `hygiene` permanently
choices.why: A prompt changes nothing in the model. It only shapes the reply to that request.

choices.text: No validation is needed once the prompt has the schema
choices.why: The model can still reply outside it; the check in the program is what catches that.

choices.text: The schema makes the model's classification of hygiene complaints correct
choices.why: It makes the label one of six words. Choosing the right one is still the model's job, and still checkable.

prompt: `repair` on `replies/fenced.txt` printed `step 2: parsed characters 47 to 166`. What did step 2 do?
hint: Where do the braces sit in the file?

choices.text: Asked the model to send the reply again without the fence
choices.why: No model is called. Step 2 is a cut, done locally.

choices.text: Removed every character that was not part of a JSON value, anywhere in the file
choices.why: It cuts once, between two braces. It does not filter characters.

choices.text: Rewrote the object to match the schema
choices.why: It never edits the object. Step 3 checks it as it is.

choices.text: Took the text from the first `{` to the last `}`
choices.why: Right. That drops the sentence, the code fence and the sign-off, and leaves the object.

prompt: Why was no second request to the model needed for `fenced.txt`?
hint: Was the answer wrong, or its wrapping?

choices.text: Lowering the temperature had already fixed it
choices.why: Temperature was never changed. The fix was a cut.

choices.text: A fenced reply is valid JSON
choices.why: It is not: step 1 failed on the first character.

choices.text: The right object was there, only wrapped
choices.why: Yes. Steps 1 to 3 cost nothing and recovered it.

choices.text: The validator skips replies that contain a code fence
choices.why: It checked the object cut from inside the fence, and found it valid.

prompt: What makes the follow-up message from `repair` on `wrong-enum.txt` more useful than "that was wrong, try again"?

choices.text: It is shorter
choices.why: It is longer. Precision is what helps.

choices.text: It contains the original complaint again
choices.why: It contains the validator's errors, not the complaint.

choices.text: It names the field and lists the allowed values
choices.why: Right. The model is told `category` and the five values, which is something to act on.

choices.text: It tells the model which category is correct
choices.why: It says which values are allowed, not which one applies.

prompt: A program retries until the reply passes the schema, with no limit. One complaint fits none of the categories, and the schema has no `other`. What happens?
hint: Is there an exit for a reply that is never valid?

choices.text: The model invents a sixth category and the validator accepts it
choices.why: The enum refuses any value it does not list.

choices.text: The loop never ends, and each attempt is billed
choices.why: Right. A reply that is never valid needs a limit, and then a recorded failure.

choices.text: The validator eventually gives up and accepts the last reply
choices.why: Validators do not give up. The loop is the caller's code.

choices.text: The model is forced to pick one of the categories, so it ends at once
choices.why: Without constrained decoding nothing forces it, and with it the loop ends but the label may be wrong.

prompt: A provider's structured output mode restricts decoding to your schema. Which statement about it is true?
hint: Shape and meaning were kept apart.

choices.text: The reply fits the schema, and that does not make its category right
choices.why: Right. It removes most of the shape failures and none of the meaning failures.

choices.text: The rules check in `rules.py` is unnecessary once the mode is on
choices.why: The refund of 140 fits the schema and still breaks the café's rule.

choices.text: Every provider names its parameters the same way, so the code is portable
choices.why: Names differ and change; the lesson says to take them from the provider's documentation.

choices.text: It lets the model write any JSON Schema feature you like
choices.why: Some modes accept only a subset of JSON Schema. Check the documentation.

prompt: Put the steps of `repair` in the order it tries them.
hint: Each step is tried only when the one before it failed.
items: Parse the reply as it is
Cut from the first { to the last } and parse that
Check the object against the schema
Print the follow-up message with the errors

prompt: `triage/7.json` passed the schema. What was wrong with `refund_amount: 140`?

choices.text: 140 is not a number
choices.why: It is a number, which is all the schema asked.

choices.text: Refund amounts have to be written as strings
choices.why: The schema says `number`, and 140 is one.

choices.text: Nothing; it matches the complaint
choices.why: It matches one number in the complaint, the wrong one.

choices.text: The customer paid R$ 70 twice, so R$ 70 is owed
choices.why: Right. The model put the whole charge in the field. Both numbers are in the complaint, and no schema knows which is owed.

prompt: According to `handbook/refunds.md`, above how many reais does a refund need the shift manager's approval?
Which of these can `rules.py` catch? Choose all that apply.
hint: It reads the triage, never the complaint.

choices.text: A refund of R$ 140, above the manager's limit
choices.why: Yes. That is its third rule, and it fired on complaint 7.

choices.text: `refund: true` with no amount
choices.why: Yes. A reply that contradicts itself is caught by its first rule.

choices.text: A refund of R$ 140 when R$ 70 was owed
choices.why: Not without the complaint. Checking against the input needs another check, or a person.

choices.text: A summary that describes a different complaint
choices.why: `rules.py` never reads the complaint, so it cannot compare the two.

prompt: In what order should a reply meant for a program be checked?

choices.text: Parse, then schema, then the café's rules
choices.why: Right. Each layer needs the one before it: no schema without a parsed object, no rule without known fields.

choices.text: Rules, then schema, then parse
choices.why: The rules read fields, which do not exist until the reply is parsed and shaped.

choices.text: Schema only, since it includes parsing and rules
choices.why: A schema needs parsed JSON first, and it does not express the café's rules well.

choices.text: Parse, then send it back to the model to check itself
choices.why: A model's view of its own reply is no evidence, lesson 5. The checks here are programs.

prompt: Match each failure to the check that catches it first.
hint: One check catches nothing in this list.

pairs.right: reading the reply against the complaint

prompt: Retries have run out and the last reply still fails the schema. What does the lesson say the program does?
hint: The complaint still has to go somewhere.

choices.text: Uses the last reply anyway, since it is the best available
choices.why: An invalid reply used anyway is the silent failure the loop exists to prevent.

choices.text: Raises the limit and keeps trying
choices.why: A limit you raise when it is reached is no limit.

choices.text: Drops the complaint without a trace
choices.why: Then nobody ever learns it failed, which is the worst outcome.

choices.text: Records the failure and sends the complaint to a person
choices.why: Right. A slower path for one complaint, with the reply and errors attached, instead of a silent hole.
